Doctor Faustus. Christopher Marlowe's tragic play about an overreaching scholar who sells his soul to the devil for forbidden knowledge and magical power, only to descend into despair and damnation. Written in the 1590s, it established the Faustian bargain as a central myth of ambition outrunning morality.

Faustus, a learned scholar, summons Mephistopheles and signs a pact: his soul in exchange for twenty-four years of unlimited knowledge and power. His famous opening speech asks, "Is not philosophy but divinity of highest kind?" The tragedy of intellectual pride seeking to transcend human limits drives the entire work.

Despite gaining magical command, Faustus's desires grow petty. He levitates spirits, pranks the Pope, squanders eternity on triviality. The play explores the Renaissance hunger for knowledge against Christian doctrine, the clash of humanism and theology that defines the era. Mephistopheles is less a tempter than Faustus's willing accomplice, even warning him as Faustus descends toward damnation.

The play uses a morality play structure in which devils and angels contend for his soul, yet it combines this with proto-modern psychology. Faustus's damnation is as much self-inflicted as imposed. His final monologue, beginning "See, see, where Christ's blood streams," depicts his last hour as the clock strikes midnight, evoking genuine terror of damnation. This meditation on mortality and regret remains one of English drama's most powerful moments.

Marlowe's only tragedy became his most enduring work, establishing the Faustian bargain—knowledge or power at the cost of the soul—as an iconic pact that would echo through literature for centuries to come.
